zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent scan reading; the returned transcription follows this copy, not a normalized headword list.

runs.text: Couſa ſuja, ou que faz aſco.

lines.note: Musai is dirty or repulsive; the Portuguese distinguishes physical dirt from something that provokes disgust.
Musamusato is labelled an adverb. The following definition concerns an imperfect, unenthusiastic manner of doing things.

runs.text: couſas imperfectamente, ou ſem goſto, nem a-

lines.note: The gloss specifies doing things imperfectly, without pleasure or application. The final a- belongs to aplicação on the next row.
Musamusato hi wo kurasu illustrates spending one’s days listlessly. The initial plicação completes the preceding Portuguese definition.

runs.text: Paßar o tempo ſem fazer nada, ou ainda q̃

lines.note: The example is translated as passing time doing nothing; the concessive clause beginning ainda q̃ continues below. Keep the abbreviation unexpanded.
The concessive clause adds that even when one does act, the work is imperfect. This is a continuation, not another entry.

runs.text: Couſa ſuja, ou que faz aſco, ou

lines.note: Musarashii is again something dirty or repulsive. The final ou introduces the additional description on the following row.
Mal composta adds the sense of being ill-arranged or untidy to musarashii; the short row completes that entry.
Musasabi is explicitly equated with Fucurô and glossed Curuja, an owl. Preserve that printed identification rather than substituting the animal associated with modern musasabi.
Musato shita koto wo yuu is saying things without consideration, as the divided Portuguese translation explains. Vt is printed italic.
Completes Di-zer: saying things without consideration. The physical division of the Portuguese verb is retained.
Musǒ is explained by yume no tsuge, a message received in a dream, and by Portuguese revelation. The headword has round s and a caron.
Vista and aparencia em sonhos complete the dream-vision definition. The gloss describes a manifestation in dreams rather than ordinary waking sight.

runs.text: O não ter renda, ou ſeruir ſem ter

lines.note: Musoku concerns lacking an income or serving without one. The next row specifies landed revenue or an equivalent provision.

runs.text: renda de terras, ou couſa equiualente.

lines.note: The absent income is revenue from land or something equivalent. This completes the definition of musoku.
Musocuna and musocuni natta describe being, or becoming, without income. The Latin alternative marker l is not Japanese.

runs.text: renda, ou terras que coſtumão ter os ſoldados.

lines.note: The gloss specifies the income or lands customarily held by soldiers, narrowing the preceding general reference to support.
A visible paragraph mark introduces another sense: musocuna or musocuno for something fruitless. The Portuguese Cou- continues below.

runs.text: ſa baldada, ou feita em vão. Vt,

lines.note: The additional sense is something vain or wasted. Muſo- begins the illustrative phrase continued on the next row.
Musocuna shinrǒ wo itaita is translated “I laboured in vain.” Preserve the printed itaita rather than substituting a modern past-tense form.
Musokunin is a person without sufficient income or maintenance. Comedia here belongs to the provision-of-support gloss, not a theatrical genre.

runs.text: baſtante que ſupra a falta do Chiguiǒ, ou rẽda.

lines.note: The maintenance must make up for missing Chiguiǒ, explicitly explained as income. This Japanese term is embedded in italic Portuguese; the final o has a caron and rẽda abbreviates renda.
Musogi denotes sixty years and is marked P. for poetic usage. The historical gi spelling is retained rather than modernized.
Musubi is the verb “tie.” The first example begins yen wo musubu, tying a bond; its Portuguese interpretation follows on the next row.
Yen wo musubu and yenpen wo musubu are glossed as marrying. The nasal abbreviations in Yẽ and yẽpẽ remain unexpanded.
Iuori wo musubu means making a hut. Mi wo then begins the separate example about a tree bearing fruit.
Mi wo musubu is bearing fruit; the upright S qualifies that usage. In- begins the next expression, about forming ritual hand gestures.
In wo musubu is described through making various movements with the hands. The Japanese phrase continues from the preceding divided In-.

runs.text: meneos, ou ceremonias como cuſtumão os

lines.note: The hand movements are compared with customary religious ceremonies. Cuſtumão is retained as the printed historical spelling.
Gentios completes the explanation of whose ritual gestures are meant. This is the dictionary’s own religious terminology, not a separate lexical entry.

runs.text: Nò, ou atadura. Cõmũmente ſe vſa

lines.note: The noun musubi means a knot or binding. Cõmũmente introduces the statement that it is commonly used in compounds.
Hitomusubi and futamusubi illustrate one knot and two knots. The examples complete the preceding statement about compound use.
Musubiague means lifting something by tying it. The divided a- begins atando, whose continuation is on the next row.

runs.text: tando aleuantar. ¶ Item, per met. Ti-

lines.note: Atando aleuantar completes the literal definition. The paragraph mark introduces a transferred use, with Ti- starting tirar.

runs.text: rar agoa de poço, ou rio. Vt,

lines.note: The transferred sense is drawing water from a well or river. Tomoni aca- begins the Japanese example about drawing ritual water together.
The example continues with aca no mizzu wo musubiague and hitotsu hachisu, drawing the water and sharing one lotus. Keep the physical split fachiſu-.
No yen to narǒ completes the wish to share that bond. The light, partly broken mark over e is read as the nasal abbreviation in yẽ; Feiq. is an upright source label and Lib. 4 is italic.

runs.text: mando agoa ( que era como benta, juntamente

lines.note: The translation describes taking water regarded as blessed. The printed opening parenthesis has no matching closing mark here; none is supplied editorially.

runs.text: ajuntar nos emos no meſmo golfão. i; Saluar

lines.note: The lotus image is translated as joining together in the same golfão and then interpreted as salvation. Enlarged reinspection shows a semicolon after i, retained as printed rather than regularized.
Nos emos completes Saluar nos emos: “we shall be saved.” This short Portuguese continuation closes the cited example.
Musubiai means joining one another. The gloss reads entre ſi, not OCR entreſio; no missing dictionary-form principal part is supplied.
Musubiauaxe is tying things together. Preserve the printed principal form ſuru even though the modern verb suggests a different expansion.
Hũas couſas com outras completes the meaning “some things with others.” The tilde belongs to u in hũas.
Musubime denotes a knot or binding. Nò carries the printed grave accent, not a Japanese long-vowel mark.
Musubisague means carrying something tied and hanging down. Dependura- has a terminal division mark and continues as dependurada below.
Da completes dependurada; the object is something hanging or tied. The preceding row’s terminal mark is not sentence punctuation.
Musubitsuke means fastening by tying. The scan reads Atando, with n, rather than OCR Atardo.

runs.text: Muſubôre, ôru, eta. S. l, Muſubore, uru.

lines.note: Musubôre and the alternative Musubore are forms for becoming tangled. Both circumflexes in the first form are visible; the S. label is upright.
The literal comparison is becoming entangled like threads. The comma after linhas connects the following &c., rather than ending the entry.
Kokoro ga musuboruru applies the tangling image to the heart; Mo- begins the Japanese explanatory equivalent continued below.
Mogiruru completes the Japanese equivalent. The Portuguese explicitly explains the figurative sense as the heart becoming disturbed.
Musuko is glossed directly as filho, a son. This is a separate short entry.
Musume is glossed directly as filha, a daughter, in parallel with the preceding entry.
Mutai is explained by tai nashi and Portuguese “unreasonable.” The Japanese explanatory phrase is not part of the Portuguese sentence.
Desaproueitada adds the sense of being unprofitable or useless to mutai. This short continuation closes the definition.
Mutaina is the adjectival form, unreasonable or unjust. The scan prints iniuſta with consonantal i here, in contrast to the descending j in injuſta- on c2-l012.
Mutaini is marked as an adverb meaning without reason. Its illustrative phrase begins again at the end of this row.
Mutaini mono wo toru or hoshigaru means taking or wanting something without justification. The alternative marker separates the two verbs.

runs.text: deſejar algũa couſa ſem razão, & injuſta-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes taking or desiring something without reason and unjustly. The final injuſta- continues into -mente below.
Mente completes injustamente, “unjustly.” Its short physical row belongs to the preceding example.
Mutsukari is glossed as crying. The usage note begins by assigning it to women’s speech; the following rows qualify that statement.

runs.text: molheres posto que tambem a vſão homens fal-

lines.note: The note says men also use the expression, despite its association with women’s speech. The divided fal- continues as fallando.
The qualification concerns speaking about children of noble status. This completes the usage restriction on mutsukari.
Mutsukarigoye denotes a tearful or crying voice. Goye is retained as the printed historical spelling.
Mutsukashii is explained as troublesome or laborious, with further detail below. The definition stresses difficulty and annoyance.
The gloss adds something that causes encumbrance or trouble. It completes the adjective before the separately printed derived forms.
Mutsukashisa is the nominal derivative, “difficulty” or “troublesomeness.” It has its own indented physical row.
Mutsukashǔ is the contracted adverbial form of the preceding adjective. Its final u carries a caron, not an ordinary unmarked vowel.
Mutsugoto is marked P. and explained as nengorona tei or affectionate words. The scan supports tei and the divided mu-, not OCR toi and mru-.
Mutsumashii kotoba nari completes the affectionate-speech explanation. The Portuguese prati- continues as pratica, conversation, not OCR praſica.
Ca familiar completes pratica familiar: intimate or familiar conversation. This closes the poetic mutsugoto entry.

The affectionate adjective is glossed as friendly or united. Enlargement confirms two final dotted i types in Mutçumaxii, rather than the more usual ij; the supplied NINJAL index independently agrees.
Amizade completes the gloss with friendship. The short continuation belongs to the affectionate adjective.
Mutsumashisa is the corresponding noun for affection or closeness. It is printed on a separate indented row.
Mutsumashǔ is the contracted adverbial form. The final u and caron are visible; OCR lost both the vowel identity and its mark.
Mutsuke describes becoming weak or wasting away. The divided emma- is continued by -grecer on the following row.

runs.text: grecer, ou definhar. Particularmente ſe diz

lines.note: Emmagrecer and definhar specify becoming thin or wasting away. The next clause explains the expression’s typical application.

runs.text: de caualos, & paſſaros que ſe crião em caſa,

lines.note: The usage note particularly mentions horses and birds raised domestically. Paſſaros retains the printed long-s sequence.

runs.text: tambem ſe diz de homẽ, maximè de mininos.

lines.note: The same expression also applies to people, especially children. Maximè is a Latin qualifier within the Portuguese note.

runs.text: Pano de linho, ou peça que ſe poẽ

lines.note: Mutsuki is a linen cloth or piece of cloth placed on a child. The next rows describe its diaper-like function.

runs.text: nas partes exteriores da criança pera que ſe

lines.note: The cloth is placed about the child’s external parts, with its purpose completed on the next row. The physical line remains intact.
The purpose is to prevent soiling. The printed çuje has a cedilla and is not normalized to modern suje.

runs.text: O não ſaber da arte de eſgrima, ou do

lines.note: Mute here means lack of skill in fencing or a game. The negative phrase O não ſaber is central to the sense.
Jogo completes the alternative to fencing. This short row is part of mute’s skill-related definition.

runs.text: O não terem as letras da

lines.note: Muten is explained by ten nashi, lacking points or marks. Tennaxi remains printed as one word.

runs.text: China, ou Iapão certos ſinaes, ou pontos por

lines.note: The missing signs or points concern Chinese or Japanese writing. Iapão is a Portuguese place-name, not a Japanese term requiring special tagging.
The signs serve to make the written characters intelligible. The clause completes the definition of unpointed writing.
Mutena or mutena hito is a person without the relevant skill. The adjective introduces an extended description of inexperience.

runs.text: be bem da arte de jogo, nem eſgrima, nem lu-

lines.note: The person lacks mastery of games, fencing, and wrestling. Lu- begins luta, divided across the following physical row.
Ta completes luta. A new transferred example, mutena hito, broadens the meaning to general incapacity; the whole row is indented continuation text.

runs.text: Homem inhabil, & que não ſabe nenhũa arte,

lines.note: The broader meaning describes an unskilled person who knows no art. The short relative construction continues below.
The person also lacks practical resourcefulness or industry. This completes the skill-related mutena entry, before the separate unpointed-text adjective.

runs.text: Liuro, ou eſcritura ſem pontos, ou

lines.note: Mutẽna concerns an unpointed book or text, corresponding to muten above. The headword has t and a nasal abbreviation over e, not OCR Mubẽna.

runs.text: ſinais por õde ſe conhecẽ as letras. ¶ Item, per-

lines.note: The missing signs aid recognition of the characters. The visible abbreviations are õde and conhecẽ; Item, per- introduces the transferred sense continued on f343.
